hypotheses.statement: Positive mood leads to asymmetric, self-serving responses to social comparison targets: assimilation to upward targets and contrast from downward targets.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: four experiments demonstrate that compared to negative mood or neutral mood participants, participants in a positive mood engage in effortful re-interpretations of ambiguously similar comparison targets so that they may assimilate to upward comparison targets and contrast from downward comparison targets.

hypotheses.statement: Ambiguous similarity information must be present for positive mood to produce self-serving interpretation.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: in Experiment 1, we tested the initial assumption of the model presented in Fig. 1: that ambiguous similarity information must be present in order for positive mood to lead to self-serving interpretations of that information.

hypotheses.statement: Negative mood produces symmetric contrast rather than asymmetric self-serving responding, ruling out a mood-congruency account.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: However, the responses of participants in a negative mood were expected to be symmetric: contrast with both upward and downward comparison others.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving responding occurs only when the similarity cue is explicitly ambiguous, not when it is explicitly unambiguous.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Because the effects of positive mood are predicted to require ambiguous information, self-serving effects were expected to occur only when similarity information was ambiguous and open to alternative interpretation.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving reinterpretation is effortful and is disrupted by cognitive load.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: When participants were under load, the positive mood effects on responses to downward comparisons were expected to dissipate, reflecting the resource-demanding nature of self-serving asymmetric interpretations.

hypotheses.statement: Mood manipulations alone do not change self-evaluations in the absence of a comparison target.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: it was important to establish that mood, and the mood manipulations we employ, are not associated with changes in self-evaluations in the absence of comparison information.

findings.quote: A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) revealed that the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001. Participants in the positive mood condition reported more positive mood (M = 7.20, SD = .93) that those in the control condition (M = 6.15, SD = .52), t(42) = 3.43, p = .001. Participants in the negative mood condition reported more negative mood (M = 4.98, SD = .98) than those in the control condition, t(42) = -3.80, p < .001.

consequence.explanation: The manipulation-check claim that mood was successfully induced in the pilot rests on an F statistic that does not follow from the means and SDs printed beside it; the significance decision is unaffected because every achievable F is more extreme than the reported one.

findings.notes: The cell ns are not printed. I derived n = 15 per group from N = 45 with three conditions and error df = 42, then re-ran the check at an unequal 12/21/12 allocation to test whether that assumption was doing the work: the reported F = 18.44 sits below the achievable interval under both allocations, so the result is not an artefact of the equal-n assumption. Innocent explanations to weigh: the F may have been carried over from a different analysis, or one of the three printed SDs may be a typo, since a larger SD lowers F. Note the direction -- the reported statistic is LESS significant than the printed data imply, which is the opposite of the direction self-serving error usually runs, and that should be stated alongside the flag.

findings.notes: I RECORDED THIS ONE RUNG BELOW THE TOOL. grim_check returned `impossible` on bound_source='stated'. The 1-7 bound is printed verbatim for Experiments 1 and 2 ('rated their own attractiveness and the target's attractiveness on seven-point scales (1 = not at all attractive and 7 = extremely attractive)'), and Experiment 3 says its attractiveness measures were 'the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2' -- so the bound reaches Experiment 3 through the paper's own cross-reference rather than through a numeral printed in that section. That single hop is why I stepped down to highly_suspicious. The competing innocent reading a reader should see: the same paragraph reports an Experiment 3 mood mean of exactly 7.33 on a scale the paper never states, and the pilot used nine-point items, so Experiment 3 may have switched to a nine-point instrument without saying so. Against that reading, every Table 2 self-evaluation cell is at most 6.75 and the downward target mean of 4.17 sits at the midpoint of a seven-point scale. Verified against the PDF (page 10): the digits read 7.33 in both sources. n = 48 is derived as half of N = 96, not printed.

consequence.explanation: Sixty of the 193 participants Experiment 4 claims to have recruited do not appear in any reported analysis, and the paper reports no exclusions, attrition or missing data, so every Experiment 4 test runs on an unexplained subset.

findings.notes: The force of this comes from the control rows: the identical df arithmetic reconciles to the stated N exactly in Experiments 1, 2 and 3, and fails only in Experiment 4, and by 31% of the sample. Innocent explanations that would resolve it and are stated nowhere in the paper: undisclosed exclusions, listwise deletion on the attractiveness measure, or a typo in the reported N. The derivation assumes the two df values come from the models the paper describes -- a 2x2x2 factorial and single-df contrasts against a hanging control -- which is exactly what the Methods say, and is the reading under which the other three experiments reconcile.

findings.notes: The paper reports no a-priori power analysis for any of its four experiments, so verify_power_analysis had nothing to reproduce; required_n was run instead to ask the design-sensitivity question, and that is the tool named in `computed`. This is context, not an error: a pair of Experiment 3 cells (12 versus 12) has less than half the sample needed to detect even a conventionally large effect (d = 0.8) at 80% power. That was the ordinary situation for 2011 social psychology and is not a defect. It is recorded because it is the other side of the effect-size finding above -- a design with this sensitivity that nonetheless returns g near 5 on every reported contrast is exactly the configuration in which selection inflates estimates, and the two should be read together. Two tails assumed: the paper states directional predictions but never states a tail convention, so I did not claim one.
